diagnostic_evidence.quote: a curve $\mu:[0, T) \to L^1_+(\Omega)$ with $\mu \in L^2(0, T; H^1(\Omega)) \cap H^1(0,T; (H^1(\Omega))^*)$ is a {\em variational solution} of \eqref{eq:mckean_vlasov_repeat}

issues.failure_explanation: Definition def:varsol_repeat requires the solution to lie in L^2(0,T;H^1(Omega)). The standing assumptions allow V = 0 and W = 0 (W = 0 is even and H-stable), in which case the PDE is the linear heat equation on the torus; there the solution from mu_0 satisfies an identity of the form int_0^T ||mu(t)||^2_{H^1} dt comparable to sum_k |mu_0(k)|^2 (1 - e^{-2 T k^2}), which is finite if and only if mu_0 is in L^2. Hence for mu_0 in L^1_+ but not in L^2, no variational solution in the sense of def:varsol_repeat exists, so the existence claim for arbitrary L^1_+ data is false; for genuinely L^1 data the cited constructions can only yield weaker solutions (e.g. sqrt(mu) in L^2(0,T;H^1), or mu in L^2(tau,T;H^1) for every tau > 0).

failure_location.quote: Under the above assumptions on $V,W,\sigma$ and any $\mu_0\in L^1_+(\Omega)$, there exists a unique variational solution $\mu(t)$ of \eqref{eq:mckean_vlasov_repeat}.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Either restrict the hypothesis to mu_0 in L^1_+ \cap L^2(Omega) (or finite relative entropy), or weaken Definition def:varsol_repeat to local-in-time regularity (mu in L^2(tau,T;H^1) for all tau > 0, equivalently sqrt(mu) in L^2(0,T;H^1)) and adjust the theorem statement accordingly.
issues.overall_effect: The existence half of the paper's well-posedness theorem fails exactly for initial data in L^1_+ \ L^2, so the theorem over-promises its data class. The control-theoretic part of the paper is formulated in weighted-L^2 neighborhoods of the equilibrium and does not rely on L^1-data well-posedness, so nothing downstream is lost once the hypothesis or the solution notion is corrected.
issues.title: Existence of variational solutions is claimed for all L^1 initial data, but the variational class requires L^2 data
issues.why_classification: The theorem is false as stated for a whole class of admitted initial data; the repair either narrows the advertised data class of the result or changes the solution notion, a limited weakening that requires no new arguments and causes no downstream loss, so it is more than a minor local patch but needs no new architecture.

issues.failure_explanation: At t = 0 the solution equals mu_0, which is only assumed nonnegative: for example mu_0 = |A|^{-1} 1_A in L^1_+ vanishes on Omega \ A, so the claim mu(t,x) > 0 for all x fails at t = 0 for such admissible data. Strict positivity is valid only for t > 0, via parabolic smoothing and the strong maximum principle.

failure_location.quote: {\bf Mass and positivity:} for all times $t \ge 0$, $\int_{\Omega} \mu(t,x) \, dx =1$ and $\mu(t,x)>0$ for all $x \in \Omega$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate the bullet as: mass is conserved for all t >= 0, and mu(t,x) > 0 for all t > 0 and all x in Omega (with mu_0 >= 0 at t = 0).
issues.overall_effect: A degenerate-case overstatement in the well-posedness theorem; the valid statement is mu(t) nonnegative at t = 0 and strictly positive for t > 0.
issues.title: Strict positivity of mu(t,x) is asserted at t = 0 for merely nonnegative initial data
issues.why_classification: A boundary-case correction that preserves the method, the valid positivity content, and every downstream use; a one-line qualification suffices.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Under the hypotheses of Theorem \ref{thm:equilibria}, and assuming that the initial condition has finite relative entropy with respect to $\bar\mu$
$\mathcal F[\mu(t)] - \mathcal F[\bar\mu] \le e^{-2\alpha t} \bigl(\mathcal F[\mu(0)] - \mathcal F[\bar\mu]\bigr)$

follow from the logarithmic Sobolev inequality induced by displacement convexity, which is rigorously proved in~\cite{malrieu2001logarithmic} for the Euclidean space $\R^d$ and is carried over the torus with periodic boundary conditions.

issues.failure_explanation: The right-hand side is not even well formed (the factor mu(.,.) is undefined); reading it as the natural ||mu(0,.) - bar mu||_{L^1}, the stated inequality is an L^1 exponential contraction with constant exactly one. This is false within the scope of the hypotheses: for V = W = 0 (admissible, since W = 0 is even and H-stable) the dynamics is the heat equation with uniform bar mu, and for mu_0 concentrated near two well-separated points the zero-mean difference f = mu_0 - bar mu loses L^1 mass at short times only by an amount exponentially small in 1/t (diffusive leakage across the wide zero set), so ||f(t)||_1 > e^{-alpha t} ||f||_1 for small t, for any alpha > 0. The method the paper invokes (displacement-convexity logarithmic Sobolev inequality) establishes entropy decay and hence, via the Csiszar-Kullback-Pinsker inequality, only ||mu(t) - bar mu||_1 <= sqrt(2 H(mu_0 | bar mu)) e^{-alpha t}, a materially different and weaker prefactor.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Restate the conclusion as ||mu(t) - bar mu||_{L^1} <= sqrt(2 H(mu_0 | bar mu)) e^{-alpha t} (or with the equivalent free-energy prefactor), following the cited LSI plus Pinsker, and correct the initial-data factor on the right-hand side.
issues.overall_effect: The quantitative statement of Proposition thm:expconv is false as written; only the qualitative exponential L^1 convergence at rate alpha, with an entropy-dependent constant, survives. No later result uses this proposition.
issues.title: Constant-one L^1 exponential contraction is false in general; the cited LSI argument yields an entropy prefactor instead
issues.why_classification: The advertised qualitative claim (exponential convergence in L^1 at rate alpha) and the method survive via a short, routine, local restatement of the constant; the stronger constant-one contraction was never used elsewhere in the paper.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: For $K\le1$ the uniform density $\mu\equiv(2\pi)^{-1}$ is the unique (and stable) equilibrium.
At the critical coupling $K=1$, it loses stability, and for $K>1$, multiple non-uniform steady states bifurcate, all translations of
\bar\mu(x) = \frac{1}{Z}\exp\Bigl(-\frac{1}{\sigma}\bigl(V(x)+ (W*\bar\mu)(x)\bigr)\Bigr)
In our notation, the noisy Kuramoto model is written as $W(\theta) = -K\cos(\theta)$, $\sigma = 0.5$, and $V(\theta) = 0$.
$\bar\mu(\theta) =\frac{\exp\bigl(2Kr\cos\theta\bigr)}{\int_\T \exp\bigl(2Kr\cos\phi\bigr)\,d\phi},$

issues.failure_explanation: The remark never fixes sigma. The paper's own self-consistency relation gives synchronized equilibria bar mu(x) = Z^{-1} exp((K r / sigma) cos x), and linearizing about the uniform state gives the first-mode eigenvalue -sigma + K/2, so the critical coupling is K_c = 2 sigma. The profile exp(K r cos x) written in the remark corresponds to sigma = 1, for which K_c = 2, contradicting the stated critical value K = 1; conversely K_c = 1 corresponds to sigma = 1/2, for which the profile should be exp(2 K r cos x), which is exactly what the numerics section later uses. No single choice of sigma makes the remark's threshold and profile simultaneously correct.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Specify sigma and make the two assertions consistent: either fix sigma = 1/2 and write the profile as Z^{-1} exp(2 K r cos x) with r = Psi(2Kr), or state the general formulas K_c = 2 sigma and bar mu = Z^{-1} exp(K r cos x / sigma).
issues.overall_effect: The illustrative remark states the Kuramoto bifurcation in an internally inconsistent normalization, so the reader cannot tell whether sigma is 1 (threshold K_c = 2) or 1/2 (profile with 2Kr). The numerics section uses the consistent sigma = 0.5 version, so nothing else is affected.
issues.title: Kuramoto remark is internally inconsistent: critical coupling K = 1 paired with the sigma = 1 equilibrium profile exp(K r cos x)
issues.why_classification: A local inconsistency in an expository remark with a forced, content-preserving correction; no theorem, estimate, or numerical experiment depends on it.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: Combining Lemmas~\ref{lem:perturb-pure} and ~\ref{lem:K-bounded} concludes the result.
(\K\phi)(x) = -\bar\mu(x)^{-\tfrac12} \int_\Omega  \bigl[\nabla\bar\mu(x)\cdot \nabla W(x-y) + \bar\mu(x) \Delta W(x-y)\bigr] \bar\mu(y)^{\tfrac12}\phi(y)\,dy.

issues.failure_explanation: The proof establishes only that Hcal has compact resolvent, which yields discreteness, finite algebraic multiplicities, and |lambda_n| -> infinity, but not reality of the eigenvalues or the existence of dense biorthogonal (generalized) eigenfunction systems. Indeed Hcal = Hcal_loc + K is not self-adjoint in general: the kernel k(x,y) = -(bar mu(y)/bar mu(x))^{1/2}[grad bar mu(x) . grad W(x-y) + bar mu(x) Delta W(x-y)] of the compact operator K fails k(x,y) = conjugate(k(y,x)) unless grad W(x-y) . grad(bar mu(x) bar mu(y)) = 0, which fails already for the non-uniform Kuramoto equilibria, so no self-adjointness shortcut is available. Reality and semisimplicity of the eigenvalues do hold for this operator, but only via an extra argument (symmetry of L in the K(bar mu)^{-1}-inner product on zero-mean functions, i.e. <L f, g>_{K^{-1}} = -<H f, g>), and completeness requires a Keldysh-type theorem for compact perturbations of self-adjoint compact-resolvent operators; neither argument is given or cited. The same unestablished facts are used in Theorem thm:hautus: real eigenvalues are implicit in solving the shape equation with real shape functions for real controls, and the biorthonormal choice <psi_j, phi_i> = delta_{ij} presupposes semisimplicity of the critical eigenvalues.

failure_location.quote:
Its spectrum consists of isolated real eigenvalues of finite multiplicity accumulating only at $\pm\infty$, i.e., $\sigma(\Hcal) = \{\lambda_n\}_{n \ge 1}$, $\lambda_n$ isolate, finite algebraic multiplicity, $|\lambda_n| \to \infty$.
    Furthermore, there exist (generalized) eigenfunctions $\{\varphi_n\}$ of $\Hcal$ and $\{\varphi_n^*\}$ of $\Hcal^*$ such that $\langle \varphi_n,\varphi_m^*\rangle = \delta_{nm}$, and the linear spans of $\{\varphi_n\}$ and $\{\varphi_n^*\}$ are both dense in $L^2(\Omega)$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Add a lemma showing that the linearized operator is symmetrizable: on the zero-mean space, L = -K(bar mu) H with K(bar mu) xi = -div(bar mu grad xi) positive self-adjoint and H f = sigma f / bar mu + W * f bounded self-adjoint on L^2, whence real semisimple eigenvalues; then invoke a standard completeness theorem (Keldysh type) for the compact perturbation K of the self-adjoint compact-resolvent operator Hcal_loc to obtain dense biorthogonal root-vector systems.
issues.overall_effect: The spectral claims used throughout Section 3 (real spectrum, biorthonormal eigenfunction pairs) rest on an unproven assertion; until the missing symmetrizability/completeness argument is supplied, the Hautus construction, the Riccati solvability, and the whole local-stabilization chain that consumes them inherit the gap.
issues.title: Reality of the spectrum and density of biorthogonal root vectors are asserted but not established, and H is not self-adjoint
issues.why_classification: The asserted facts are true and the repair is a contained but nontrivial additional lemma plus a standard completeness theorem; no conclusion changes and no new global architecture is needed, yet the gap exceeds a routine local patch because the operator is genuinely non-self-adjoint.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: $0 = \int_\Omega \Lcal y\,dx = \langle (\A+\D_W)y,\bar\mu\rangle_{L^2_{\bar\mu^{-1}}}, \quad \forall y \in \Space,$
Since $\Pcal$ commutes with $\Lcal$ (mass conservation), it follows that $\Pcal_H$ commutes with $\Hcal$.

issues.failure_explanation: From int_Omega L y dx = 0 for all y one correctly obtains bar mu in ker(L*) in the weighted space X = L^2(bar mu^{-1}), the kernel of the adjoint; the proof then asserts bar mu in ker(L), which does not follow because L is not self-adjoint on X (cf. the non-symmetric kernel of K in ISSUE-005), so the two kernels are different objects. The asserted membership is true: L bar mu = div(bar mu grad(sigma + W * bar mu)) = 0 using the equilibrium identity sigma grad bar mu = -bar mu grad v[bar mu], but it requires this separate direct computation, which is missing. The final conclusion 0 in sigma(L) is already valid from ker(L*) nontrivial, but the fact bar mu in ker L is exactly what is needed later for 'P commutes with L' (i.e. L P = L) in the zero-mean reduction.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace 'so bar mu in ker(L)' by the direct computation: div(bar mu grad W * bar mu) = div(bar mu grad v[bar mu]) - div(bar mu grad V) = -sigma Delta bar mu - div(bar mu grad V) = 0, hence L bar mu = 0.
issues.overall_effect: A broken inference inside the proof; the proposition's conclusion and the downstream zero-mean projection framework survive once the short direct computation of L bar mu = 0 is added.
issues.title: Invalid inference from bar mu in ker(L*) to bar mu in ker(L) for the equilibrium direction
issues.why_classification: The erroneous step is repaired by a short, routine direct computation; all conclusions and downstream constructions are preserved.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: By \autoref{lem:spectrum_finite}, the spectrum of $\Lcal$ in the half-plane $\Re\lambda\ge -\delta$ consists of exactly $m < \infty$ eigenvalues $\{\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_m\}$.
\bigl\{\lambda\in\sigma(\Lcal) : \Re(\lambda) \ge -\delta\bigr\}

issues.failure_explanation: The hypothesis only says that some 'first' m eigenpairs lie in the closed half-plane Re lambda >= -delta; it does not exclude further critical eigenvalues. If sigma(L) intersected with {Re lambda >= -delta} contains more than m eigenvalues, the hypothesis holds while the conclusion fails: at any additional critical eigenvalue, an eigenfunction phi of L* satisfies B* phi = (<psi_j, phi>)_j = 0 by biorthogonality with the eigenfunctions of L at other eigenvalues, so ker(lambda I - L*) cap ker B* is nontrivial and the Hautus condition (hence delta-stabilizability) fails. The proof's first sentence already asserts 'exactly m' critical eigenvalues, but Lemma lem:spectrum_finite provides only finiteness, so exhaustiveness must be part of the hypothesis; as stated, the theorem's hypothesis does not imply its conclusion.

failure_location.quote: Assume the first $m$ eigenpairs $\{(\lambda_j,\psi_j)\}_{j=1}^m$ of $\Lcal$ satisfy $\Re\lambda_j \ge -\delta$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Strengthen the hypothesis to: the spectrum of L in {Re lambda >= -delta} consists of exactly m eigenvalues (counted with algebraic multiplicity), with eigenpairs {(lambda_j, psi_j)}_{j=1}^m.
issues.overall_effect: The theorem as literally stated is false; with the intended 'exactly m' hypothesis the proof goes through. All results that rest on delta-stabilizability (the Riccati proposition and, through the closed-loop stability it provides, the maximal-regularity, contraction, and local-decay results) inherit the gap.
issues.title: Hautus theorem does not require the m eigenpairs to exhaust the critical spectrum
issues.why_classification: A missing one-phrase hypothesis that the proof already assumes and uses; once added, the method, the conclusion, and the advertised scope all survive unchanged.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: The equation has a solution $\beta_j \in W^{2,p}(\Omega)$ for any $p > 0$, if and only if the right-hand side is orthogonal to the kernel of $\Hcal_{\mathrm{loc}}^\dagger = \Hcal_{\mathrm{loc}}$
$\langle f, \bar\mu \rangle_{L^2_{\bar\mu^{-1}}} = \int_{\Omega} f(x) \, dx = 0$

issues.failure_explanation: For the self-adjoint elliptic operator Hcal_loc with one-dimensional kernel span{sqrt(bar mu)}, the Fredholm solvability condition for Hcal_loc beta_j = -sigma varphi_j is orthogonality <varphi_j, sqrt(bar mu)> = 0, not varphi_j not in span{sqrt(bar mu)}: a right-hand side with a nonzero component along sqrt(bar mu) is not in the span, yet the equation has no solution. The stated criterion is therefore wrong as written. The conclusion is nonetheless correct, because <varphi_j, sqrt(bar mu)>_{L^2} = <psi_j, bar mu>_{L^2_{bar mu^{-1}}} = int_Omega psi_j dx = 0 since the eigenfunctions psi_j lie in the zero-mean space X_0, exactly the content of Remark remark:kernel_L0; so solvability holds for the actual right-hand sides.

failure_location.quote: Therefore, the equation is solvable if and only if $\varphi_j \notin \operatorname{span}\{ \sqrt{\bar\mu} \}$, or equivalently, $\psi_j \notin \operatorname{span}\{ \bar\mu \}$, which is true by \autoref{remark:kernel_L0}.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace 'if and only if varphi_j not in span{sqrt(bar mu)}, or equivalently, psi_j not in span{bar mu}' by 'if and only if <varphi_j, sqrt(bar mu)>_{L^2} = 0, equivalently int_Omega psi_j dx = 0, which holds since psi_j in X_0'.
issues.overall_effect: An incorrect intermediate equivalence in the proof; the solvability of the shape equation, and hence the theorem's construction and conclusion, are unaffected.
issues.title: Fredholm solvability of the shape equation is misstated as non-membership of the kernel span instead of orthogonality to the kernel
issues.why_classification: The misstated criterion is immediately repairable using the zero-mean property already recorded in Remark remark:kernel_L0; no conclusion or construction changes.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: is the same, since $\B^* 1 = 0$.
which implies $\Lcal^* \bar\mu = 0$
\Pcal y = y - \Bigl(\int_{\Omega}y\Bigr)\bar\mu,

issues.failure_explanation: In the weighted space X = L^2(bar mu^{-1}) used in this paper, ker(L*) = span{bar mu}, P* = P with P bar mu = 0, and B* bar mu = (int_Omega B_j dx)_j = 0; whereas for the constant function 1: L* 1 is nonzero (e.g. <L y, 1>_{bar mu^{-1}} = int bar mu^{-1} L y dx does not vanish in general), P 1 = 1 - |Omega| bar mu is nonzero, and B* 1 = (int_Omega grad alpha_j . grad log bar mu dx)_j is nonzero in general. Consequently Pi = P* Pi_0 P + gamma 1 1* does not solve (R_full) for gamma nonzero (the terms (L* + delta P*) Pi + Pi (L + delta P) do not annihilate the gamma-part), and the claimed invariance of the feedback 'since B* 1 = 0' fails. The statement matches the unweighted-L^2 setting, where the constants are the neutral direction; in the present weighted setting the correct extension is Pi = P* Pi_0 P + gamma bar mu bar mu*, and the feedback invariance holds because B* bar mu = 0.

failure_location.quote: any solution $\Pi_0$ of~\eqref{eq:riccati_reduced} lifts to a family of solutions of \eqref{eq:riccati_full} by $\Pi = \Pcal^*\Pi_0 \Pcal + \gamma 1 1^*$, for all $\gamma \in \R$, where $1$ indicate the constant functions.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Replace the constant direction 1 by bar mu throughout the claim: Pi = P* Pi_0 P + gamma bar mu bar mu* solves (R_full) for all gamma in R, and the feedback law is unchanged because B* bar mu = 0.
issues.overall_effect: The asserted equivalence between the full-space Riccati equation and the reduced one is wrong as stated. The operative objects, the reduced equation (R_0), Proposition prop:ARE posed on X_0, the feedback u = -B* Pi y, and the numerical computations (which solve the reduced finite-dimensional ARE), are unaffected.
issues.title: Full-space Riccati lift uses the constant direction 1, but in the weighted space the neutral direction is span{bar mu} and the claimed identity B* 1 = 0 is false
issues.why_classification: A forced, local correction of the neutral direction in an auxiliary equivalence claim; the reduced ARE, the feedback law, and all guarantees and computations remain intact.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: \Hcal_{\Pi} = \Hcal - \delta I + \hat\B \hat\B^{*} \hat\Pi, \quad \hat\B=\unitary \B, \quad \hat\Pi=\unitary\,\Pi\,\unitary^{-1},
Additionally, the operator $\Lcal_{\Pi} \coloneqq \Lcal + \delta I - \B \B^* \Pi$ generates an exponentially stable semigroup on $\Space_0$.

issues.failure_explanation: With A = lambda I - Hcal_loc and B = -(delta I - B^ B^* Pi^ + K) one obtains A + B = lambda I - Hcal_loc - delta I + B^ B^* Pi^ - K, which equals neither H_Pi = Hcal_loc + K - delta I + B^ B^* Pi^ nor the generator -H_Pi of the stated Cauchy problem (wrong sign of the unbounded part and of K, plus a spurious lambda I), so the reduction of the equation to the cited maximal-regularity theorem is invalid as written. Moreover, the theorem's conclusion on the whole half-line, a global W(Q_infinity) estimate valid for every psi_0 in L^2_0, requires exponential stability of the semigroup generated by -H_Pi: otherwise already the free evolution from a non-decaying eigenmode leaves W(Q_infinity). This ingredient is available in the paper through Proposition prop:ARE via the unitary equivalence -H_Pi = U L_Pi U^{-1}, but it is never invoked in the proof.
issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Decompose the generator instead: -H_Pi = A + B with A = Hcal_{loc,lambda} (sectorial, D(A) = D(Hcal_loc) cap L^2_0) and B = -(lambda I + K - delta I + B^ B^* Pi^) bounded on L^2_0, apply the cited bounded-perturbation maximal-regularity theorem, and invoke prop:ARE (exponential stability of L_Pi, transported by the unitary U) to extend the estimate to (0, infinity).
issues.overall_effect: The proof does not establish the stated maximal-regularity estimate as written; the statement itself is correct (sectorial decomposition of the generator plus the exponential stability from prop:ARE), and it is the basis for the contraction argument of thm:nonlin-existence and the decay claim of thm:local-decay.
issues.title: Maximal-regularity proof uses a decomposition that does not reconstruct H_Pi and never invokes the exponential stability needed on the half-line
issues.why_classification: The conclusion is correct and every needed ingredient exists in the paper; the repair is a local rewrite of the proof's decomposition together with an explicit citation of prop:ARE, with no change to any claim or guarantee.

diagnostic_evidence.quote: for the confining potential \(V(x)=0.05\cos(2x)\) and interaction \(W(x)=-\cos x\)
For a high temperature, e.g. $\sigma \ge 0.78$, the unique steady state is $\bar\mu(x) \propto e^{-\cos(2x)/\sigma}$.

issues.failure_explanation: The text specifies the experiment with V(x) = cos(2x), while the caption of the figure reporting the same experiment uses V(x) = 0.05 cos(2x). The reported phenomenology, in particular the bifurcation temperatures sigma approximately 0.77-0.78 at which 'two other steady states emerge', depends quantitatively on this amplitude, so the experiment as described is not reproducible: one of the two parameter specifications is wrong, and the source does not determine which.

failure_location.quote: Set $V(x)=\cos(2x)$ and $W(x)= -\cos x$, and a variable temperature $\sigma$.

issues.least_adequate_overall_repair: Make the amplitude consistent between text and caption (state the value actually used in the simulations) and, if necessary, restate the corresponding threshold temperatures.
issues.overall_effect: The numerical claims of the cosine-potential paragraph (threshold temperatures and the heatmap of Figure fig:kuramoto_potential_control_heatmap) cannot be matched to a uniquely specified model.
issues.title: Inconsistent confining-potential amplitude between text and figure caption in the cosine-potential experiment
issues.why_classification: A parameter inconsistency in the description of one numerical experiment; it does not touch any theorem or the control methodology, but it admits two distinct corrections and affects the reproducibility of the reported thresholds.
